newsitem.title: USA: Reservation system set for Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Reservation system set for Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case announced on Tuesday a telephone reservation system for the more than 2,000 bombing victims to obtain one of 325 seats for a closed-circuit telecast of the trial.

U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch said in a written order that bombing victims, including relatives of the dead and injured, must call a toll-free number two days before they wish to attend a trial session by telecast on a particular day.

Congress mandated that the trial be telecast to Oklahoma City for bombing victims and their families, after the case was moved to Denver. Victims had complained that it would be too expensive for many of them to travel to Denver.

The telecast will be in a government auditorium secured by armed guards. Twelve seats for victims also will be set aside in the Denver courtroom where accused bomber Timothy McVeigh is to go on trial March 31.
The trial date for co-defendant Terry Nichols has not been set. They were accused of the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building which killed 168 people and injured 500.

After 315 victims call for seats on a particular day no more reservations will be accepted for that day, Matsch said. Ten seats will be set aside for victims who live outside Oklahoma and for elderly or handicapped people, he said.
More than 2,000 people are listed as victims in Justice Department records. The department is required by law to assist crime victims.

Separately, a federal appeals court in Denver refused Tuesday to reconsider its ruling that allowed the judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial to ban some victims from court proceedings. The ban applies to victims who will be death-penalty witnesses if either defendant in the bombing case is convicted.
Only two of the 12 judges of the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals favoured reconsidering last month's ruling by a three-judge panel of the court which upheld the ban.

About 80 victims of the bombing and the Justice Department petitioned the court to reconsider. Forty-nine U.S. senators and representatives, supporting victims' rights, joined the request as "friends of the court."
The court gave no reason for refusing to reconsider.
The bombing case judge issued the ban last year, citing a federal court rule that prohibits people from attending court proceedings if they are to be witnesses.

The Justice Department and victims argued that the rule should not apply in cases where the victim will testify only in a penalty phase of a trial. The rule is designed to prevent witnesses from being influenced by what they hear or see in court.
